source.title: The Growing Pains of Frontier Models: When Leaderboards Stop Separating and What to Measure Next

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper briefly characterizes neural scaling laws as predicting aggregate loss, but its own analyses concern benchmark-score coupling and capability transitions, not held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on benchmark coupling across models and sizes, not the loss-scaling behaviors named in V1–V7. Section 5.2's coupling values are recorded as related but distinct findings; claims about scaling laws in Related Work are background, not the paper's results.
record.test_reason: The paper measures correlations between benchmark scores (SWE-bench vs GPQA, plus HLE and IFEval) across frontier models, and a 'net coupling' quantity across open-weight model sizes. It reports no held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute, and no fitted loss laws or compute-optimal splits. It also reports no downstream performance against scale or loss. Scaling laws appear only as one Related Work paragraph.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that frontier capabilities cooperate (r = +0.72), with lab-specific slopes and residuals (the h-field) that show recipe emphasis and pivots. They also claim a second coupling transition at 30–72B parameters. They frame the work as complementary to loss scaling laws, not a test of them.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures public benchmark-score coupling and residuals rather than fitting neural language-model loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that coupling depends on subset definition and sufficient dynamic range on both benchmark axes; these sensitivities concern its benchmark-coupling analysis, not loss-law fits.

fits_no_version.finding: In OPT, net coupling between benchmark capabilities rises from 0.514 at 125M to 0.876 at 13B, falls to 0.356 at 30B, and recovers to 0.396 at 66B. Llama-2-70B, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B and OLMo-2-32B show low coupling of 0.18–0.22.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-benchmark capability coupling changes non-monotonically with model size, weakening around 30–72B parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 34 frontier models, SWE-bench and GPQA Diamond scores correlate at r = +0.72. This is a correlation between benchmarks, not a relation to scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frontier benchmark capabilities are positively correlated across labs.

record.problems: The paper says it does not run evaluations itself; frontier scores are predominantly self-reported, independent verification lags, the panel is lab-imbalanced, and the Nc,3 evidence is preliminary (n = 4). It does not report loss-scaling measurements relevant to this claim.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation of small-run loss fits to much larger runs.
Effect of architecture shape on loss at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance against scale or pretraining loss. Only cross-benchmark correlations are reported.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Nothing in the study bears on any version; the T6 relation 'discusses' is appropriate. Coupling values in Section 5.2 may be drawn from the companion paper (arXiv:2605.18838) rather than measured here.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small-run loss fits predict much larger runs.
Loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
The effect of architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling beyond text pretraining.
Downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents, allocation trends, or curve shape on setup and fitting choices.
